title: Nelson Mandela: An Ideal for Which I Am Prepared to Die
summary: 'I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination. I cherish the ideal of a democratic and free society... it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.'
keywords: Nelson Mandela: An Ideal for Which I Am Prepared to Die
full_text:
On April 20, 1964, inside the Palace of Justice in Pretoria, Nelson Mandela stood in the dock facing the gallows.

The apartheid regime had charged him and his comrades with high treason. Rather than pleading for mercy or allowing his lawyers to mount a technical legal defense, Mandela delivered a four-hour statement from the dock that shook the conscience of the world.

Addressing the judge without a trace of fear, Mandela concluded with his immortal manifesto:

"During my lifetime I have dedicated myself to this struggle of the African people.
I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination!
I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities!

**It is an ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve.
But, my Lord, if needs be...
It is an ideal for which I am prepared to die!**"

Silence descended upon the courtroom. The judge was visibly unnerved. Fearing international condemnation and internal insurrection if Mandela was executed, the court sentenced him to life imprisonment on Robben Island.

For twenty-seven years, confined to a damp eight-by-seven-foot cell and forced to break stones in a lime quarry, Mandela's spirit remained unbroken.

In 1994, he walked out of prison to be inaugurated as the first democratic President of South Africa. His courage proved that when a leader is prepared to die for human dignity, no prison walls can arrest the march of freedom.
moral: True moral conviction transcends the fear of death; an ideal rooted in justice is indestructible.
